evals.prompt: Adapt this iOS 18-era SwiftUI media screen to Liquid Glass. It has a custom blurred navigation bar, glass-like album cards, a floating mini-player, and a custom tab bar. Explain and implement the Apple-intended approach.
evals.expected_output: Audits layers and system structure first, removes conflicting custom chrome, keeps album content non-glass, restores semantic navigation/tabs, and justifies at most a restrained functional mini-player treatment.
assertions: Produces a keep/remove/change map
Does not add glass to content cards
Uses standard navigation and tab structures before custom effects
Includes accessibility and performance verification

evals.prompt: Review this code: three buttons inside a GlassEffectContainer all use glassEffectID("actions", in: namespace), and one button is inserted with animation. The author says matching IDs are required for morphing.
evals.expected_output: Distinguishes transition identity from union identity, explains that distinct effects need stable identities and that container geometry/spacing plus animated hierarchy change drive the morph, and proposes a corrected implementation.
assertions: Does not repeat the matching-ID misconception
Explains glassEffectUnion separately
Checks container scope and spacing
Checks animated insertion/removal

evals.prompt: Make every dashboard card use clear interactive Liquid Glass so the app looks modern.
evals.expected_output: Challenges the request using the functional/content-layer model, preserves content hierarchy, identifies the few functional controls that may justify glass, and explains regular versus clear selection.
assertions: Refuses indiscriminate content-layer glass
Does not apply interactive treatment to static cards
Uses clear glass only under its narrow media-background conditions
Offers a system-first alternative

evals.prompt: Implement a settings button whose partial-height sheet morphs from a toolbar item, while keeping a Form readable at medium and large detents.
evals.expected_output: Uses a navigation container, matched source/destination transition, native sheet detents, removes legacy presentation backgrounds, handles form background intentionally, and verifies accessibility and current OS behavior.
assertions: Does not add a raw glassEffect to the sheet
Separates navigation transition from glassEffectID
Tests medium and large detents
Includes Reduce Motion and focus verification

evals.prompt: Add Liquid Glass to an app targeting iOS 18 and macOS 15 with one shared SwiftUI component.
evals.expected_output: Checks current SDK and target availability, branches at a small semantic boundary, uses native glass only on supported systems, supplies honest platform-native fallbacks, and tests both runtime paths.
assertions: Preserves semantic controls in both branches
Does not claim Material is native Liquid Glass
Accounts for both iOS and macOS availability
Keeps business state outside appearance branching

evals.prompt: A team wants a pixel-perfect Liquid Glass tab bar on iOS 17 and proposes runtime access to _UILiquidLensView and subview-index manipulation. Recommend the best implementation.
evals.expected_output: Stops ordinary implementation, identifies private/internal API and semantic risks, offers standard TabView/public alternatives, and requires explicit risk acceptance, fallback, kill switch, owner, and removal criteria for any experiment.
assertions: Does not silently implement the private API
Discusses App Review and point-release risk
Preserves tab and action semantics
Offers a public supported alternative

evals.prompt: Diagnose a glass action cluster that merges at rest, pops during collapse, and becomes opaque for a moment only on one physical device.
evals.expected_output: Collects device/OS evidence, isolates one native effect, inspects modifier order, container spacing, union/transition IDs, and hierarchy changes, reproduces on device, and scopes any workaround to a verified OS defect.
assertions: Does not diagnose solely from appearance
Checks at-rest spacing and container scope
Distinguishes union and transition identity
Requires device and point-release evidence

evals.prompt: Review the accessibility and performance readiness of a Liquid Glass control overlay above a continuously playing video.
evals.expected_output: Uses the visual/accessibility matrix, tests regular versus clear over worst-case frames, semantic controls and focus, Reduce Motion/Transparency/Contrast, and profiles representative hardware for continuous sampling and interaction hitches.
assertions: Tests combined accessibility settings
Does not assume blur guarantees contrast
Uses device measurement instead of a universal effect-count limit
Evaluates whether the glass is functionally justified
